items.prompt: Black's bishop on f8 is free now that the e-pawn has moved. Tap every square it attacks (squares holding its own pieces count).

claims.statement: The bishop on f8 attacks exactly these squares.

hints: Look at the diagonal that runs from f8 towards the queenside.
The e7 square is empty now; the g7 pawn is also on a diagonal of the bishop.
a3, b4, c5, d6 and e7 on one diagonal, plus g7.
items.explain: The bishop on f8 moves along two diagonals. The e7 square is empty after ...e6, so the long one toward a3 is open: a3, b4, c5, d6, e7. The other diagonal has its own pawn on g7, which still counts as attacked (defended).

items.prompt: Now the bishop on c8. Tap every square it attacks (own pieces count).

claims.statement: The bishop on c8 attacks exactly these squares.

hints: Which of its two diagonals leaves the board at once?
The pawn on e6 stands on its long diagonal.
b7 on one side; d7 and e6 on the other, and the diagonal stops at e6.
items.explain: The c8 bishop sees b7 (own pawn) on one side and d7 and e6 (own pawn) on the other. The pawn on e6 closes the long diagonal toward h3, so after ...e6 this bishop is hemmed in until it moves or the pawn does.

items.prompt: Black has just played the b8 knight to d7 and White's bishop has moved to c4. Is the Black king in check?

claims.statement: Black is in check.

hints: Draw the diagonal from c4 to the king.
Name every square between the bishop and the king.
d5 and e6 are empty, so nothing blocks the bishop.
items.explain: The bishop on c4 looks along d5 and e6 to f7, where the king stands. No piece is between them, so it is check. Black must move the king, capture the bishop, or put something on d5 or e6.

items.prompt: Same position, but the e-pawn stands on e6 instead of e7. Is the Black king in check?

claims.statement: Black is not in check.

hints: The only change from the last board is the pawn on e6.
Look at the squares between c4 and f7.
The pawn on e6 stands on that diagonal.
items.explain: The bishop on c4 now meets the black pawn on e6 before it reaches the king, so there is no check. The bishop attacks the pawn instead.

items.prompt: White's queen now eyes the pawn on e6. How many Black pieces defend that pawn?

claims.statement: Exactly one black piece attacks (defends) the square e6.

hints: Count the black pieces that could capture on e6 if a white piece stood there.
The queen on d8 and the king on g8 do not reach e6.
Follow the diagonal from c8.
items.explain: Only the bishop on c8 guards e6, along d7. The king is on g8 and the queen on d8 does not see the square. One defender means the pawn depends on that bishop staying where it is.

items.prompt: White's knight on g6 attacks the rook on h8 and the bishop on f8. Black to move: find a reply that keeps Black clearly better; several work.

claims.statement: Engine, depth 16: these five replies are within 90 centipawns of the best and keep Black clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: ...Rh7 is at least 50 centipawns worse than the best move.

hints: The knight on g6 is far from its friends. What can attack it, or what can Black do while it sits there?
One reply strikes at the white centre; another attacks the knight directly.
...c5 hits the d4 pawn; ...Qe8 attacks the knight on g6; ...Bd7, ...Nbd7 and ...Qd5 develop.
items.explain: The knight on g6 forks the rook on h8 and the bishop on f8, but it is lonely and the king is safe on g8. Engine, depth 16: ...c5, ...Bd7 and ...Qe8 are the closest to best, and several other developing moves also keep Black clearly better; the exchange costs Black little.

feedback_by_move.h8h7: Saves the rook but leaves the f8 bishop to a knight that is not trapped; Nxf8 is a trade of knight for bishop, and the engine rates ...Rh7 at least 50 centipawns worse than the best reply.

items.prompt: White has pushed g4. Find a developing reply; several work.

claims.statement: Engine, depth 16: after ...Bd6 Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: after ...Bb4+ Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: ...Nxg4 is at least 100 centipawns worse than the best move.
Engine, depth 16: after ...Qb6 Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: after ...Nd5 Black is clearly better.

hints: Black's f8 bishop is free. Which diagonal squares give it something to do?
One move gives check; the other eyes the h2 pawn and the white king's side.
...Bb4+ checks; ...Bd6 develops with tempo on the h2 pawn.
items.explain: The bishop on f8 can move now. ...Bd6 and ...Bb4+ both develop it with a point. Taking on g4 with the knight loses time and lets White open lines against a king that has no pieces nearby. Engine, depth 16: ...Nxg4 is worse than either bishop move by more than a pawn.

feedback_by_move.f6g4: Grabs a pawn but pulls the knight away from the centre and gives White the g-file and a quick rook lift; the engine rates it more than a pawn worse than the bishop moves.

items.prompt: Same setup as the trap board, with one change: Black answered with the other knight, from f6 to d7. White to move: find the winning move.

claims.statement: White mates in one with the queen capture on e6.

hints: Which Black piece used to defend e6?
The knight on d7 now blocks the bishop's line to e6.
The queen takes the pawn with check; look at h7 and f8.
items.explain: The c8 bishop's only route to e6 runs through d7, and the knight now stands there. So e6 has no defender, and Qxe6+ is check with the bishop on d3 covering h7 and the bishop on f8 and rook on h8 boxing in the king on g8: checkmate.

items.prompt: White has the queen on e2 and the bishop on d3. Black to move: find a safe move.

claims.statement: Engine, depth 16: these thirteen moves are within 100 centipawns of the best and keep Black ahead.
After ...Nbd7 White mates in one.
After ...Nfd7 White mates in one.

hints: Count the guards of e6 after your move.
Any move except the two knight moves to d7 is worth a look: count the guards of e6 after your move.
...c5, ...Bd7, ...Na6, ...Qc7, ...Nd5 and several other developing moves keep a guard on e6 or leave it alone.
items.explain: The pawn on e6 is attacked by the queen and guarded once. Moving a knight to d7 shuts the bishop's line and leaves nothing guarding e6; nearly every other move is fine, and the key lists the ones the engine rates within a pawn of the best.

feedback_by_move.b8d7: Blocks the bishop's path to e6: Qxe6 is checkmate.
feedback_by_move.f6d7: Also blocks the path to e6: Qxe6 is checkmate.

items.prompt: White's queen on d3 faces Black's queen down the d-file, and White has just captured on c5. Does ...Qxd3 trade queens without losing material?

claims.statement: After ...Qxd3 Bxd3 neither side is ahead on material.

hints: Who recaptures on d3?
Compare what Black takes with what Black loses.
White's bishop recaptures; queen for queen.
items.explain: Queen takes queen, bishop takes queen: a plain even trade. Material stays level after the trade, and White's most dangerous attacker, the queen, is gone.

items.prompt: The same position with White's queen and bishop swapped: the bishop stands on d3 and the queen on d1. Does ...Qxd3 trade queens without losing material?

claims.statement: After ...Qxd3 Black loses the queen for a bishop.

hints: What defends the piece on d3 this time?
Count the white pieces that attack d3.
The queen on d1 and the pawn on c2 both guard d3.
items.explain: The bishop on d3 is defended by the queen on d1 and the pawn on c2, and the capture only wins a bishop for a queen. Count the defenders before offering a trade.

items.prompt: Black to move: find a good move in the position of the last contrast.

claims.statement: Engine, depth 16: after ...Qxd3 Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: after ...Nbd7 Black is clearly better.

hints: White's knight on e5 and the pawn on c5 are the obvious targets.
One move trades the queens; one develops and keeps the queens on.
...Qxd3 trades; ...Nbd7 attacks the knight.
items.explain: ...Qxd3 removes White's queen, the piece that makes the knight on e5 dangerous. ...Nbd7 develops and challenges the knight but leaves the queens on. Engine, depth 16: both are close.

items.prompt: White to move after 5...h6 (the position on the last two boards). Compare 6.N5f3 (the retreat) with 6.Nxf7. Which description fits the engine at depth 16?

answer.outcome: the capture leaves White about two pawns worse
options: the capture leaves White about two pawns worse
the capture leaves White about four pawns worse

After the capture on f7 and the recapture the engine rates White between 1.2 and 2.3 pawns worse.

hints: Count material after each move.
A knight for a pawn costs about two pawns of material, but White gets some activity back.
The retreat gives up nothing.
items.explain: The retreat keeps both knights and gives up nothing. The capture gives a knight for a pawn. Engine, depth 16: the retreat is within a pawn of equal; the capture leaves White about two pawns worse.

items.prompt: White has checked with the bishop. Black to move: find a reply that keeps Black clearly better.

claims.statement: Engine, depth 16: after ...Be6 Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: after ...e6 Black is clearly better.
Engine, depth 16: after ...Nd5 Black is clearly better.

hints: Which Black pieces can step between the bishop and the king?
A pawn and a bishop can both block.
...e6 with the pawn, ...Be6 with the bishop, or ...Nd5 with the knight.
items.explain: The check can be blocked on e6 or d5. The engine ranks ...Be6 slightly higher than the pawn move, but the lesson follows ...e6 because the plans after it are the ones shown here; ...Nd5 also holds.

items.prompt: The bishop is on d3, the king on g8, the queen on e2 and Black's knights stand on d7 and f6. Does Qxe6 win at once?

claims.statement: White mates in one with Qxe6.

hints: Which piece defended e6 and where is it now?
Count the squares the king can reach on g8.
h7 is covered by the bishop on d3.
items.explain: The king on g8 cannot capture on e6 and the bishop on c8 is blocked by the knight. After Qxe6+ the king has no free square, so it is mate.

items.prompt: The same position, with one change: the king stands on f7 instead of g8. Does Qxe6+ win?

claims.statement: After Qxe6+ Kxe6 White has lost the queen for a pawn.

hints: Which piece defends e6 this time?
The king itself is next to e6.
The king on f7 simply takes the queen.
items.explain: With the king on f7, the king itself defends e6 and the bishop on d3 does not, so Qxe6+ Kxe6 just loses the queen. The trap needs e6 to be undefended once the bishop's line is blocked; here the king is a second guard.
